item.title: Bio-logger development
item.description: Our work in bio-logger development is driven by a simple idea: if we want to understand behaviour in the wild, we need devices and analytical systems that are built around the biology of the question, not only the engineering of the sensor. We have worked across the full pipeline, from Daily Diary methods and behaviour annotation to logger optimisation, data transmission, and multi-sensor system design. This includes work on how to deploy tags more effectively for movement ecology, how to recover richer behavioural information from onboard sensors, and how to move large quantities of data reliably from free-ranging animals. Together, these projects have helped build the methodological foundation for extracting behaviour, performance and ecology from increasingly complex biologging systems.

item.title: Biophysics of flight
item.description: Our work on soaring birds focuses on the physical limits of flight, the aerodynamic challenges birds face when negotiating complex airflows, and the use of onboard sensors to quantify individual flight performance in free-ranging animals. Using high-resolution bio-logging, particularly inertial measurement units, GPS, magnetometers and related movement sensors, we investigate how birds climb, glide, turn and adjust their behaviour under changing atmospheric conditions. This allows us to recover fine-scale measures of performance from flight itself and to link body motion to flight strategy, space-use and proxies of energetic expenditure.

item.title: Katherine Steinfield
item.description:
Social Soaring Scavengers

Katherine is an ecologist and ornithologist interested in how environmental change influences animal movement and space use. Working within the long-term Andean condor field system in Argentina, she studies how social interactions shape the movement strategies of soaring scavengers navigating mountainous energy landscapes. By combining biologging data with ecological field research, her work also explores how human-driven environmental change may influence movement costs, space use, and the ecological dynamics of these iconic species.

item.title: Dr. Hannah Williams
item.description:
Hannah J. Williams is a behavioural ecologist whose research focuses on the fundamental processes that shape movement decisions in animals. Leader of the Move.inFormation research group at the University of Konstanz as a VolkswagenStiftung Freigeist Fellow.

Her work explores how organisms navigate complex environments in which the energetic consequences of movement are uncertain and constantly changing. By integrating behavioural ecology with physics and information theory, she investigates how animals perceive environmental energy, how they use social cues to reduce uncertainty, and how these processes shape movement patterns across scales.
